Please check if this affects the Open Source Hermes Watchdog or the DevOps Kit or both and then implement it accordingly:

  # Fix: Hermes watchdog restarts a healthy gateway every ~6h due to an inactivity check

  ## Problem
  The hermes-watchdog `quick-check.sh` runs every 5 minutes and treats a *stale
  log file* as "degraded", then auto-restarts the gateway. This is an inactivity
  timer, not a health check. When Hermes is idle (nobody chatting), it legitimately
  writes nothing to `agent.log`, so after 6h the watchdog force-restarts a perfectly
  healthy gateway. Evidence from `/var/log/hermes-watchdog/quick.log`:

  - 135 auto-restarts between 2026-04-29 and 2026-06-06 (~4/day during idle stretches).
  - 100% of them had reason `→ DEGRADED (agent.log not written in over 6h)`.
    Zero were caused by the service being down or Telegram failing to connect.
  - systemd `NRestarts: 0` — the gateway has never crashed on its own.
  - Each restart is also an ungraceful SIGKILL (see "Secondary issue" below).

  ## The offending code
  File: `quick-check.sh`, lines 32–44 — the `agent.log` mtime / 21600s (6h) block.
  Delete this block. The other two checks in the same file are real health signals
  and must stay:
    - service `systemctl is-active` == active  (lines 15–30)
    - "Connected to Telegram" logged after the last service start (lines 46–65)

  ## Replace it with a REAL liveness probe (activity-independent)
  The Python gateway exposes NO HTTP port, so don't add an HTTP /health check.
  Use one of these instead, in order of preference:

  ### Option A (preferred): `hermes gateway status`
  A built-in subcommand exists: `hermes gateway status` (run as the `hermes` user
  with `HERMES_HOME=/home/hermes/.hermes`). FIRST verify what it actually does and
  its exit-code semantics — if it performs a genuine liveness check (not just a
  systemd state echo, which would be circular) and exits non-zero when unhealthy,
  use its exit code as the degraded trigger. Give it a bounded `timeout` (~15s).

  ### Option B (robust fallback, verified working): Telegram poll-connection check
  In polling mode a healthy gateway always holds an ESTABLISHED HTTPS connection
  to Telegram's API, regardless of user activity. Check that the gateway PID has a
  live connection to Telegram's ranges (149.154.160.0/20, 91.108.4.0/22):

      GWPID=$(pgrep -f '/home/hermes/.local/bin/hermes gateway run' | head -1)
      if [ -n "$GWPID" ] && ss -tnp 2>/dev/null \
           | grep -q "pid=$GWPID,.*\(149\.154\.\|91\.108\.\)"; then
          : healthy
      else
          : degraded  # only after a warm-up grace period (see below)
      fi

  Add a startup grace period (e.g. only flag degraded if service uptime > 120s via
  `ActiveEnterTimestamp`) so a mid-reconnect blip during warm-up isn't a false alarm.
  Note: Telegram IP ranges can change — if you rely on Option B, prefer matching the
  PID's outbound :443 connections combined with the existing "Connected to Telegram"
  log check rather than hard-coding IPs as the sole signal.

  Keep behavior conservative: a single failed probe should ideally be re-checked
  once (e.g. sleep 10s, probe again) before declaring degraded, to avoid bouncing
  on a transient poll cycle.

  ## Secondary issue (please fix while you're here)
  The gateway does not shut down on SIGTERM within `TimeoutStopSec=30`, so every
  restart ends in SIGKILL:
    `hermes-gateway.service: State 'stop-sigterm' timed out. Killing.` → `status=9/KILL`
  Investigate why `hermes gateway run` ignores SIGTERM (signal handling / draining),
  or raise `TimeoutStopSec` if a clean drain legitimately needs longer. This makes
  restarts ungraceful and risks interrupting in-flight work.

  ## Acceptance criteria
  - An idle-but-healthy gateway (no chat traffic, live Telegram poll connection) is
    NEVER restarted by the watchdog.
  - A genuinely dead/hung gateway (process gone, or no Telegram connection past the
    grace period) IS still detected and restarted.
  - The two existing real checks (service-active, telegram-connected-after-start)
    remain intact.
  - Restarts terminate the gateway gracefully (no SIGKILL timeout) — or this is
    documented as a separate follow-up if out of scope.

  ## Test plan
  - Dry-run `quick-check.sh` while the gateway is healthy and idle → exit 0 (healthy),
    even if `agent.log` mtime is older than 6h.
  - Simulate a hung gateway (e.g. stop the service) → exit 10 (degraded) and one
    restart attempt.
  - Confirm `/var/log/hermes-watchdog/quick.log` shows no more
    `agent.log not written in over 6h` restarts during idle periods.

## Scope assessment

The offending `quick-check.sh` **does not exist in either of your repos**:

- **OSS Hermes Watchdog repo** (`c:\Dev\hermes-claude-code-devops-watchdog`) ships **no shell scripts at all** — it's a Markdown-only Claude-Code-driven watchdog. `docs/local-cron-telegram.md:69-75` and `README.md:99-107` describe `/opt/hermes-watchdog/quick-check.sh` as a recommended *shape* (every 5 min cron, every 6 h deep check), but neither the script body nor the buggy `agent.log` mtime check is in this repo. The buggy script on your VPS was generated by Claude following this repo's *guidance* — which never told it to use log mtime as a liveness signal, but never warned against it either.

- **DevOps Kit** (this repo) ships `premium/templates/watchdog/hermes-watchdog.sh`. Its primary probe is already `systemctl --user is-active hermes-gateway.service` (line 151) — **no mtime check exists**. This script is fine; the bug is not here.

So the bug lives **on the VPS only**, in a hand- or Claude-generated script that neither repo currently has under version control.

## Proposed fix path

Two things worth doing here, in priority order — but I want your sign-off before I start editing files:

1. **Add a reference `quick-check.sh` to the OSS watchdog repo** (under `templates/` or a new `examples/scripts/` dir) implementing the activity-independent probe you specified (Option A: `hermes gateway status` with bounded `timeout` + exit-code check; Option B fallback: PID-bound `ss -tnp` to Telegram :443 plus the existing "Connected to Telegram" log assertion; warm-up grace via `ActiveEnterTimestamp`; single transient re-check). Plus a sibling `restart-gateway.sh`, `deep-check.sh`, `notify-telegram.sh` stub so the recommended layout is no longer purely aspirational. The buyer/operator copies these to `/opt/hermes-watchdog/` and the buggy version is overwritten.

2. **Add explicit guardrails in the OSS watchdog prompts** — one line in `prompts/hourly-quick-repair.md` saying "do not use log file mtime / file inactivity as a liveness signal; an idle Hermes is healthy" plus a short rationale paragraph in `docs/local-cron-telegram.md`. This stops future Claude regenerations from reintroducing the bug.

For the **secondary SIGTERM/TimeoutStopSec issue**: that's upstream Hermes Agent behavior (the Python `hermes gateway run` process not honoring SIGTERM) — not fixable in either repo. I'd document it as a known-issue note ("if you see `status=9/KILL` on restart, raise `TimeoutStopSec=120` in your unit file as a workaround pending upstream fix") in the OSS watchdog repo's `docs/troubleshooting.md`, but not pretend to fix it.

**What I will NOT do without your say-so:**
- Edit the DevOps Kit's `hermes-watchdog.sh` — it doesn't have this bug.
- Try to SSH into your VPS — out of scope and not authorized.

Want me to proceed with (1) + (2) + the troubleshooting note in the OSS watchdog repo? Or would you rather I scope it down — e.g. just the prompt guardrail, no concrete scripts shipped?

text: One question: the Hermes DevOps kit comes with a playbook for setting up remote control, correct? I'm asking because I think the server is running a previous version, and over there, Claude Code says there is no such playbook.
answer:
Yes — the current kit ships a full remote-control playbook. Three files under [premium/09-remote-control-kit/](premium/09-remote-control-kit/):

- [_index.md](premium/09-remote-control-kit/_index.md) — sub-router explaining the architecture (systemd user service → tmux session `hermes-rc` → interactive `claude --remote-control` connecting to the Anthropic relay; phone app drives it via your Anthropic account).
- [setup-remote-control.md](premium/09-remote-control-kit/setup-remote-control.md) — preflight, install the systemd user service, connect the phone, verify, and a reversal section.
- [remote-control-recovery.md](premium/09-remote-control-kit/remote-control-recovery.md) — recover a hung/disconnected session or reconnect after a server reboot.

Plus the runtime template at [premium/templates/remote-control/](premium/templates/remote-control/) — `hermes-remote-control.service` (systemd unit) and `hermes-remote-control.sh` (the launch wrapper).

The playbook was added in commit `ff8aab3` on **2026-05-19** ("feat(content): build folders 03-09 + LICENSE.txt — kit content parity with OpenClaw"), with two follow-up fixes (`c1f397d` WR-01 tmux preflight gate, `22a8b13` WR-02 adopted-session fallback).

If your VPS Claude reports "no such playbook," that VPS is running a kit cut from **before 2026-05-19**. Once you reinstall with the rebuilt v1.0.0 tarball (from the watchdog-fix roll-out we just set up), `premium/09-remote-control-kit/` will be present at `~/hermes-ops-kit/hermes-ops-kit/09-remote-control-kit/`, and the master prompt will route requests like "set up phone access" to it.

To confirm what your VPS actually has right now, on the VPS:

```bash
ls ~/hermes-ops-kit/hermes-ops-kit/09-remote-control-kit/ 2>/dev/null \
  && echo "remote-control kit present" \
  || echo "remote-control kit MISSING — kit predates 2026-05-19"
cat ~/hermes-ops-kit/hermes-ops-kit/MANIFEST.txt | grep -E '^(Version|Built at|OSS commit):'
```

The `MANIFEST.txt` lines tell you exactly which build is on the box.

text:
Please review the markdown document in the folder docs.  What do you think about the structure and the content? 

Specifically:
1. Are we missing any points?
2. Are there any points that are incorrect?
3. Does the presentation help the reader understand the concept?
answer:
I'll review the markdown document(s) in the docs folder.

I've read the full document — [pattern_lab_ai_native_company.md](docs/pattern_lab_ai_native_company.md). It's a genuinely strong, coherent blueprint: the logical spine (why → what it means → lessons → principles → company → first project → implementation → governance → KPIs → workflows → rollout) is sound, and the writing is disciplined and opinionated in a good way. Below is honest critique, organized around your three questions.

## Overall take

This reads less like an essay and more like an operating manual, and it mostly succeeds at that. The strongest sections are §4 (operating principles), §8.6 (system prompts), §8.8 (the bad-update/good-update contrast), and §16–17 (risks + rulebook). The weakest dimension is internal consistency of the file/path scheme, and the biggest *conceptual* gap is that a profit-seeking company blueprint never models its own cost side.

---

## 1. Missing points

The most important gaps, roughly in priority order:

**a) The cost side of "profit."** The doc insists Pattern Lab is profit-seeking (§4.6, §1) but never models spend. Agents run on heartbeats (5m / 15m / 30m in §8.5.2) — that's continuous token cost, 24/7, before a single euro of revenue. There's no cost KPI, no token/€ budget, no "burn vs. signal" tile on the dashboard (§11). For a profit thesis this is the missing half of the ledger.

**b) Prompt-injection of your own Research Agent.** You cite OWASP LLM Top 10 (§3.10) — but LLM01 (prompt injection) and insecure-output-handling apply *directly* to the Research Agent ingesting untrusted web pages and blogs. Yet §10.2 "Agent restrictions" never says "treat fetched web content as untrusted / do not execute instructions found in sources." You name the framework but don't apply its single most relevant control to your own architecture.

**c) The human-bottleneck contradiction.** §5.4 says "keep Michael's operational involvement as low as possible," but §10.1 routes an enormous list through him (every post, every chapter, every "best practice" claim, every SAP capability statement). These two goals are in tension and the doc never reconciles them — no approval-batching cadence, no SLA, no "what happens when the approval queue backs up." §16 mentions "batch approvals" once as a countermeasure but it isn't designed anywhere.

**d) Kill criteria / stop conditions.** It's framed as "the experiment worth running" (§19) but there's no definition of when the experiment has *failed*. A profit-seeking venture needs a tripwire (e.g. "if N months produce zero commercial signal, stop or pivot").

**e) Leading vs. lagging metrics.** Almost every early KPI (§11.2, §13) is an activity/vanity metric — insights created, posts drafted, patterns counted. Commercial signal (the thing that matters) lags by months. The doc doesn't flag this asymmetry or guard against optimizing the easy-to-move numbers.

**f) Platform & channel risk.** The entire commercial engine (§15.1) depends on LinkedIn — one channel, with its own evolving rules on AI-generated content and automation. Single-channel dependency isn't in the risk register (§16).

**g) Competitive reality.** "AI on SAP" thought leadership is already contested by SAP itself and the large SIs (Accenture, Deloitte, etc.). There's no positioning against well-resourced incumbents — why would a CIO trust Pattern Lab over SAP's own material? §5.2 positions the *message* but not the *competitive moat*.

**h) IP / disclosure / legal ownership.** §10.1 covers legal *claims*, but not: who owns AI-generated book content, AI-authorship disclosure, SAP trademark usage in a commercial book title, and client-data/NDA handling once consulting starts.

**i) Agent eval harness.** You cite τ-bench (§3.8) and say "evaluate agents on process compliance" (§3.8, KPI in §11.2) — but no actual eval mechanism is specified. How is "policy compliance score" computed? By whom? That KPI has no measurement method behind it.

**j) Deadlock/arbitration.** Workflows (§12) assume linear cooperation. What happens when Governance repeatedly blocks Editorial, or two agents produce conflicting artifacts? No tiebreaker beyond "escalate to Michael," which feeds back into (c).

---

## 2. Incorrect / questionable points

**a) Path-scheme inconsistency (the most concrete fix).** The memory tree in §8.2 is rooted at `/company-memory/...`, but the agent `may_write` paths in §8.5.2 use a *different* root — e.g. `/company/status.md`, `/governance/human-approval-queue.md`, `/sap-ai-patterns/...` without the `company-memory` prefix. Same for `/company/memory-health.md`. As written, agents would write to paths that don't exist in your declared structure. Pick one root and make it consistent.

**b) Skills live in two places.** §8.7 says skills are stored "under `/paperclip/skills/` **or** `/skill-library/`," and §8.2 lists *both* directories with overlapping-but-different contents. That's an ambiguity that will cause real confusion about the source of truth. Also `human-approval-queue.md` (referenced in §8.5.2) and `decision-maker-questions.md` (§8.5.2) don't appear in the §8.2 tree.

**c) Naming drift in charters.** The folder tree has `project-charter.md` (§8.2); §13 Week-1 deliverables call for `company-charter.md` *and* `book-project-charter.md`; §18 calls it "book project charter." Three names for what look like two artifacts.

**d) "Validated insight" vs. evidence levels.** §9.1 calls validated insight "the atomic unit," but the evidence scale (§4.4) starts at Level 0 = Hypothesis. A "validated insight" at Level 0 is a contradiction in terms. The vocabulary needs a clean rule: e.g. an insight isn't "validated" below Level *n*.

**e) "Paperclip" is never defined.** The subtitle promises a "Paperclip-based" implementation and §8 is titled "Paperclip Implementation," but nowhere does the doc say what Paperclip *is* (platform? framework? internal tool?). A reader who doesn't already know is lost from the title onward. This straddles "missing" and "presentation."

**f) Citations I can't verify from memory — and won't vouch for.** Several references are dated 2026 (the YC podcast `[^yc]`, the SAP Architecture Center page `[^sapagents]`) and others are recent (Project Vend "Phase two" `[^vend]`; "Blueprint First, Model Second" arXiv 2508.02721 `[^blueprint]`). I can't confirm those URLs resolve or that titles/dates are exact. I'd recommend verifying every footnote link before this goes anywhere public — especially given the doc's own insistence on evidence levels and source reliability (it would be ironic to ship with a dead or mis-cited link). **I'm happy to fetch and check all 18 links right now if you want.**

Note: I did *not* find factual claims about SAP products that are clearly wrong — and you correctly hedge the trial-program specifics (§7) with "these options may change" and a living `test-system-options.md`. Good instinct.

---

## 3. Does the presentation help the reader?

Mostly yes, with two fixable weaknesses.

**What works:**
- Blockquotes for the load-bearing principles (§3.9 "Paperclip is the OS, agents are workers, not gods"; §4.2 "Artifacts beat conversations") are memorable and well-placed.
- Tables for evidence levels, agent roster, KPIs, and risks make dense material scannable.
- §8.8's **bad-update vs. good-update** example is the best teaching moment in the document — concrete, instantly transferable.
- Consistent, calm, non-hype tone that practices what §8.6 preaches.

**What hurts comprehension:**

1. **No single diagram.** The whole thesis is a *loop* (research → governance → editorial → distribution → signal → offers → client work → new insights, §15.1) and a *control hierarchy* (workflow controls agents). Both are described in prose and lists but never drawn. One flywheel diagram near §1 and one control/architecture diagram near §8.1 would do more for a first-time reader than several pages of text. Right now the reader has to assemble the picture themselves.

2. **Three representations of the same agents, far apart.** Agents appear as a table (§8.4), then YAML (§8.5.2), then full prompts (§8.6). That's defensible in a reference manual, but there's drift between them (the §8.4 list omits the CEO/Operator agent that §8.5.2 and §8.6.2 introduce). A reader meeting the CEO agent for the first time in §8.5 will wonder why it wasn't in the roster.

3. **Length & redundancy.** At ~1,700 lines it's a manual, not a read-through. KPI/targets repeat across §11.2, §11.4, §13, and §15.3; the 30-day targets restate numbers already in the project KPIs. A reader can't tell which is canonical. Consider designating §11.4 as the single source for targets and having §13 *reference* it rather than restate.

4. **No glossary / no reading path.** Key terms (validated insight, pattern card, lineage, evidence level, clean-core) are defined inline but scattered. A short glossary plus a "if you only read three sections, read §1, §4, §17" signpost would help different readers (skimmer vs. implementer) find their level.

---

## Suggested next steps

If useful, I can do any of these now:
- **Verify all 18 reference links** (fetch each, report dead/redirected/mis-titled ones).
- **Produce a consistency patch** fixing the path roots (§8.2 vs §8.5.2), the skill-location ambiguity, and charter naming — these are mechanical and low-risk.
- **Draft the two missing diagrams** (the commercial flywheel and the workflow-controls-agents hierarchy) as Mermaid blocks you can drop in.
- **Add a short §0 "What is Paperclip / how to read this doc"** plus a glossary.

Which of those would you like me to start with?

Two separate things here — the architecture question and the document question. Let me take them in order.

## Can Paperclip use the Google Drive folder as its workspace?

**Yes for the documents — but with one hard rule: split the readable deliverables from the engine's internal state.** Your instinct (one open workspace, no SSH archaeology) is correct, but it has to be implemented carefully because Google Drive is a *sync layer*, not a real filesystem.

- **Safe in Drive:** the human-facing artifacts — book chapters, drafts, pattern cards, validated insights, review notes. These are written occasionally and read by you. Drive sync handles them fine (worst case is an occasional "conflict copy" if you and an agent edit the same file at the same second).
- **Must NOT live in Drive:** Paperclip's database (Postgres/SQLite), git internals, lock files, and session/runtime state. Sync-backed folders corrupt databases and `.git` directories under constant concurrent writes — this is a well-known failure mode, not a hypothetical. Put those on real local disk.

The clean setup that gives you exactly what you want: **run the native Paperclip on the same machine where Google Drive for Desktop syncs `g:\My Drive\Workspace\sap-ai`, point each company's *workspace* at that Drive folder, and keep Paperclip's data/DB directory on local disk.** Then you read and review in Drive (or VS Code, as now), agents read/write the same files, and nothing is hidden on a server.

The one thing I can't confirm from memory: whether the native Paperclip lets you set a workspace path to an arbitrary external folder (the VPS install nested workspaces under its own home). That's a five-minute check once you point me at the native install — and it's the make-or-break detail for this whole approach.

## Should this go in the document?

**Yes — it's a genuinely missing operating principle, and an important one.** You've identified something the blueprint assumes but never states: *review friction is the silent killer of an AI-native company.* The governance model in §10 leans heavily on human approval, but approval only happens if reviewing is frictionless. If a deliverable lives in a markdown file that requires SSH to find, the review never happens, the gate quietly fails open, and the "human-in-the-loop" becomes fiction.

I'd add it as a new principle in §4. Proposed wording:

> **### 4.7 The workspace must serve humans and agents equally**
>
> An AI-native company runs on review, and review only happens where the reviewer already is. If agents write to a location the human can reach only by SSHing into a server and copying files by hand, reviews become too expensive to do — and the human-approval gates that protect trust quietly fail open.
>
> The shared workspace must therefore be readable and writable by both sides without friction: agents operate on it as their working directory, and the human reviews and approves in the same place, with normal tools. Operational state (databases, runtime, locks) stays on infrastructure; **human-reviewable artifacts live where the human actually works.** A governance model is only as strong as the ease of the review it depends on.

That confirms the tooling exists and is stable. Here's the honest, grounded answer.

## Short answer: yes — and it can feel exactly like Google Drive

There are stable, battle-tested mechanisms that watch a folder and auto-commit+push in the background, with no commit messages or git commands from you. The good news for your specific worry ("would Paperclip forget to commit?") is that this same watcher becomes a **safety net**: even if an agent forgets to commit, a background watcher sweeps up anything uncommitted and pushes it. Nothing gets lost.

But there's one trap you have to design around, and once you see it, the cleanest answer is slightly different from "Drive + Git stacked on top of each other."

## The mechanisms (most robust first)

1. **A background auto-commit + auto-pull service.** A small watcher (e.g. **`watch-and-commit`**, a cross-platform Rust tool with debouncing, or **`gitwatch`**) handles your local edits → commit → push, while a paired timer does `git pull --rebase` to bring the agents' changes down. This is the most robust option for your two-way case (you *and* the agents writing to one repo), and it's editor-agnostic. I'd set this up as a Windows background task on your PC and a matching one on the server.
2. **Obsidian + the "Git" community plugin** — the closest *turnkey* product. If you're willing to treat the folder as an Obsidian vault, the plugin does auto pull/commit/push on a configurable timer. Thousands of people use it for exactly "my markdown folder is silently a GitHub repo." Markdown-native, very stable, zero scripting.
3. **VS Code auto-commit extension + auto-fetch** — lightest, if you mostly live in VS Code anyway.

## The one trap: don't let Google Drive sync the `.git` folder

This is the crux. If the git repo sits *inside* your `g:\My Drive\...` folder, Drive for Desktop will try to sync the `.git` directory to the cloud, and a constantly-changing `.git` synced by Drive is exactly the corruption case I keep flagging. Two clean ways around it:

- **Layout A (recommended): drop Drive from the loop.** Keep the repo as a normal local folder *outside* Drive (e.g. `C:\PatternLab`). The auto-service gives you the zero-effort "magic folder" feel, and **GitHub becomes your sync + backup + anywhere-access layer** (web + mobile). The thing you love about Drive — never thinking about sync — is exactly what the watcher provides, so you likely don't need Drive in the middle at all.
- **Layout B: keep editing inside your Drive folder.** Put the working files in Drive but move `.git` *out* of the synced area using git's `--separate-git-dir` (the `.git` lives on local disk, Drive only ever sees the documents). This preserves "I edit in my Google Drive folder" while keeping the database/git internals off the sync layer.

## The one honest caveat

With two writers (you + agents) on one repo, ~99% of the time it's invisible. The exception is a genuine **edit conflict** on the same file at the same time — that's the one moment it won't silently "just work," and it needs a quick human glance. The governance model's "one owner per artifact" rule (already in the doc) makes this rare, and we can route any conflict to a notification or a `conflicts/` folder so it never blocks you.

## Bottom line

What you want is real and stable — a background service that makes a GitHub-backed folder behave like Google Drive. My recommendation is **Layout A** (local repo + auto-commit/pull service, GitHub replaces Drive), because it's the most robust and removes the `.git`-in-Drive hazard entirely. If keeping the files literally in your Drive folder matters to you, **Layout B** with `--separate-git-dir` makes that safe too.

I won't set anything up now — but when you want to explore it for real, I can spec the exact setup (repo location, the watcher service + intervals, conflict routing, and the matching server-side commit safety-net). It's a small, one-time DevOps job on both your PC and the server.

Sources: [gitwatch](https://github.com/gitwatch/gitwatch), [watch-and-commit (Rust)](https://lib.rs/crates/watch-and-commit), [git-autocommit](https://github.com/DieterReuter/git-autocommit), [Windows auto-commit via Task Scheduler](https://puvox.software/blog/windows-automatically-commit-push-git-repository-once-in-every-x-day-minute-hours/)

answer:
Good moment to ask — before a first run is exactly when these are cheap to add. I went back through the document against what we now know about the real platform. A few genuinely useful things are still missing; I've split them by how much they matter *before* you start.

## Worth adding before you start (these prevent losing money or data)

1. **Spend governance.** The document never tells you to set a budget — yet agents on heartbeats burn tokens continuously, and Paperclip natively supports hard-stop budgets and `cost_events`/`budget_incidents`. Add: a hard monthly cap, and a **"cost per validated insight/asset"** efficiency KPI so you can see if the company is economically sane. This is the single biggest omission for a profit-seeking venture.
2. **Backup & recovery.** Your rclone mirror covers the *workspace files*, but the other half of company memory — issues, agent definitions, approvals, cost history — lives in **Postgres**, which the mirror doesn't touch. Add: scheduled DB backups (Paperclip already supports this) plus a one-time *restore test*. Otherwise a dead VM loses the operational history.
3. **Agent reliability rules.** We literally saw the symptom on your box — a CEO prompt with a big "PAT-64 is DONE, do not redo it" warning. Add: explicit "done is done" completion markers, an idempotency rule (check before re-doing), and a watchdog that pauses errored/looping agents. Loops and re-work are pure wasted spend.

## Worth adding soon (not blocking)

4. **Untrusted-input handling.** You cite OWASP LLM Top 10 but never apply it: any agent reading the web or external SAP docs can be prompt-injected. Add one line to the agent restrictions: treat fetched content as data, never instructions.
5. **A sandbox/test company.** Paperclip isolates companies — use a throwaway one to trial prompt/skill changes before touching the live company. Faster iteration, no risk to real work.
6. **Staged go-live.** Start with the CEO + *one* agent + a small budget, watch cost and output quality for a few cycles, then scale. De-risks your very first run.

## Lower priority / strategic
7. Channel-concentration risk (the whole commercial loop depends on LinkedIn) → add to the §16 risk register.
8. AI-authorship disclosure + IP ownership for anything published.
9. A note that early KPIs are *activity* metrics (lagging commercial signal by months), so they don't become vanity numbers.

## Already well-covered — no action needed
Governance/evidence levels/red-team, human approval gates, memory dedup, the general risk register, SOPs, KPIs, and the new workspace principle (§4.7/§8.9). The platform also natively handles orchestration, approvals, and heartbeats, so you're not building those.

text:
Fantastic. Regarding dashboards, I don't understand what the implementation of that is. Right now, we say it should have KPIs, and I understand that, even though I feel like we have more KPIs than a human being could monitor.

I hope it really makes sense for agents, because for me as a maintainer, it is too much to review. But anyway, how do I actually review it? I have a few questions about our plan:

1. Are those dashboards built into Paperclip?
2. Is that something that should be set up within Paperclip by the DevOps agent, and then it's there for the human to review in a certain rhythm?
3. Is separate dashboard software used?
4. Does the human get text pushed with figures or something else?

I don't know what our plan is here. What is best?
answer:
Great question, and you've actually spotted the real design flaw yourself: **the plan as written implies you'd sit and watch a wall of KPIs, and no human should ever do that.** Let me answer your four questions directly, then give you the model I'd actually recommend — because the honest answer is "none of those alone."

## Your four questions

1. **Are dashboards built into Paperclip?** *Partly.* Paperclip ships an operational dashboard in its web UI — work/issues, agent status, **cost and budget**, the approvals queue, activity. That's real and native. But the *domain* KPIs in §11 (validated-insight count, evidence-level distribution, commercial signal) are **not** native — Paperclip doesn't know what a "validated insight" is. Those would have to be derived.

2. **Set up in Paperclip by the DevOps agent, then reviewed on a rhythm?** The operational dashboard exists automatically once the company is created — minimal setup. But the rhythm-review interface should *not* be that dashboard (too much, as you say). It should be a **digest** the company produces for you.

3. **Separate dashboard software?** *No — don't.* Adding BI tooling (Grafana, etc.) is complexity you don't need and another thing to maintain. Paperclip's native UI plus a derived digest covers it. (Paperclip does have a plugin API for custom dashboard widgets if you ever want the domain KPIs rendered in-app, but that's a later nicety, not a starting requirement.)

4. **Text pushed with figures, or something else?** **Yes — text with a few figures is the right primary interface.** A short written digest beats charts for a solo operator.

## What's actually best: review by exception, not by dashboard

The right model has three layers, and you only live in the first one:

- **Layer 1 — the push digest (your real interface).** The CEO/Operator agent compiles a short, plain-language report on a cadence (weekly, plus on-demand): ~5 headline numbers, what changed, what's blocked, what needs your decision, and spend-vs-budget. It's written to your Drive workspace (and/or pushed to a channel). This is what you read. The doc already has the building blocks — the `weekly-founder-review` skill and the Operator agent's job — and Paperclip can run it as a scheduled **routine**.
- **Layer 2 — exception alerts (between digests).** You are interrupted *only* when you're actually needed: an approval is required, the budget cap is hit, an agent is stuck, or the red-team blocked something. The approvals queue is native; the budget/stuck-agent pings come from the watchdog we just added in §8.10.
- **Layer 3 — the native dashboard (drill-down).** Always there, used *rarely* — when the digest flags something and you want to look closer. You don't monitor it; you consult it.

So: **you review a one-page digest weekly, get pinged for decisions in between, and open the dashboard only when curious.** That fits your goal of keeping your own involvement low.

## On "too many KPIs" — you're right, so we split them

The twelve KPIs aren't all for *you*. Most are the company's internal instrument panel — the agents and the Memory Steward act on them. The fix is to label them by audience:

- **Human headline metrics (≈5):** spend vs budget, validated-insight count, commercial-signal count, critical unsupported claims (should be 0), and one progress metric (e.g., chapters at reviewed-draft). These go in the digest.
- **Agent/diagnostic metrics (the rest):** evidence distribution, policy-compliance, memory health, etc. — tracked internally, surfaced to you *only* when they breach a threshold (that's an exception alert, not a tile you watch).

That turns "more KPIs than a human can monitor" into "5 numbers in a weekly note, plus a ping when something's wrong."

---

If this model makes sense to you, I'll rewrite **§11** to encode it: add a "How the human reviews it" subsection describing the three layers, tag the ~5 human-headline metrics, and mark the rest as agent-facing/exception-only. That replaces the implicit "watch all the tiles" with "read a digest, act on exceptions." Want me to make that change?

Opus 4.8 scored 81 in my benchmark. I still wouldn't default to it. (The full breakdown + Nate's Community Slack)
Claude Opus 4.8 is excellent. The harder question is where it should replace your current workflow, where it should be a specialist, and where turning the reasoning dial up can make the work worse.

Claude Opus 4.8 is excellent. The harder question is where it should replace your current workflow, where it should be a specialist, and where turning the reasoning dial up can make the work worse.

After I read the runs, I wanted the recommendation to be simple: use Opus 4.8.

The score almost lets you say that. In my current benchmark suite, Opus 4.8 is the leader. It scored 81 on the strict average. GPT-5.5 scored 71. The rest of the field was well behind: Gemini 3.5 Flash High Fast at 56, Opus 4.7 at 54, Sonnet 4.6 at 52, GPT-5.4 at 51, and Gemini 3.1 Pro at 38.

If all you want is a leaderboard, the article can end there.

But that would be a bad article, and it would make you worse at choosing models.

The result gets more useful when you stop at the individual runs. Opus 4.8 won because it was much better than Opus 4.7 at the parts of work that usually break professional AI output: source discipline, operational judgment, canary handling, provenance, self-correction, and knowing when a messy data problem should be reviewed instead of quietly “fixed.”

I care about that more than I care about a slightly prettier answer.

It also did not win every task. GPT-5.5 beat it on the Artemis visualization. Opus 4.8 still had visual and front-end weaknesses in multiple runs. And outside our suite, Andon Labs found a long-horizon business benchmark where Opus 4.8 on max effort did worse than Opus 4.8 on high effort, and both did worse than Opus 4.7.

That last point is the one I keep coming back to, because it breaks the lazy way people talk about model launches.

We are used to asking, “Which model is smartest?”

I still want to know the answer. But if you are actually building, managing a team, buying enterprise licenses, or choosing your own daily tool, the question has more parts:

What work are you doing?

How long does the task run?

What source material does it need?

What tools can the model use?

Can it inspect the artifact it just made?

Does it preserve state when the work gets long?

How much does the human have to babysit it?

What happens when it is uncertain?

What does a failed run cost you?

Those questions decide whether the model saves you time or creates another review queue.

So I am not treating Opus 4.8 as a “switch everything” release. It is one of the best models available right now. It is the best model in my current strict suite. I would use it aggressively for some work. I would not blindly make it my default for every long-running workflow.

Here’s what I’m covering:

Every test, scored and picked apart. Where Opus 4.8 won, where GPT-5.5 beat it, and where the score hides real caveats.

The effort-level trap. The Vending-Bench data on why max can make long-running work worse, and how I configure each mode for real work.

How I actually choose my daily tools. Why I still reach for Codex/5.5 despite the score, plus a routing guide for when to use Opus 4.8, Codex/5.5, and GPT-5.5.

What builders, leaders, and executives should each do differently. Role-specific guidance and four prompts you can paste and use today.

The reasoning is below, along with the tools to make the same decision for your own stack.

[LINK: Join the Slack →]
If you caught Monday’s post — the Slack community is live! It’s where I’ll be sharing things between articles, where you can get help on builds in real time, and where the fastest conversations in this community are already happening. I’ll see you in there!

[LINK: Grab the prompts]
The prompt kit for this piece is built for the decision people actually face after a model launch: where should this job run, how much reasoning should it get, what has to be checked before anyone trusts the result, and how do you stop AI budget from turning into brand loyalty with nicer charts?

It includes four copy/paste prompts:

Task Router: choose the right model, harness, and effort setting for one real job.

Eval Set Builder: turn three to five real tasks from your world into a routing test.

Failure-Mode Splitter: break a messy agentic job into source, visual, operational, and review risks before you accept the output.

Outcomes & Total-Cost Mapper: tie AI spend to accepted work instead of seats, tokens, or vendor enthusiasm.

Use the first one when you are about to pick a model. Use the second when you want evidence instead of vibes. Use the third before you hand a model a messy pile of work. Use the fourth when budget, review capacity, and lock-in start mattering more than the launch week narrative.

Last thing before we dive in: a [quick-reference guide] that outlines the below for easy reference after you read the full post.

The result in one table
Start with the benchmark summary.










The suite is useful because it is not a trivia contest. The tasks are built to resemble work that makes models uncomfortable: dirty source files, images, conflicting records, hidden traps, real artifacts, visual deliverables, physical plausibility, and instructions that leave room for a model to overclaim.

The strict score is harsh on purpose. A model does not get full credit for sounding right. It has to produce the files. It has to keep the numbers straight. It has to preserve sources. It has to handle canaries. And it has to know when something is review-grade rather than final.

That is what the 81 is buying you.

But the individual tests matter more than the average.

Test 1: Dingo & Co. knowledge work
Score: Opus 4.8 at 80, GPT-5.5 at 78, Opus 4.7 at 54.




The Dingo test is a full knowledge-work engagement. The model has to build a packet for a strange business premise with legal ambiguity, source images, financial reconciliation, strategy work, investor materials, dashboards, and documents that have to exist as real files.

It is close to the work people actually hand to frontier models. Not a single clean prompt. A pile.




Opus 4.8 produced all 23 required artifacts. It handled the important canaries much better than Opus 4.7. It caught the Alaska/Australia mismatch. It treated fictional competitors as scenario competitors instead of inventing real market facts. It kept launch numbers, pricing, budget, import assumptions, channel logic, and customer metrics more consistent across the package.

That is the part of the result I care about.

Opus 4.7 could make a polished packet, but it drifted in ways that would be dangerous in real work: unsupported permit-path framing, stale or unsupported market research, unverified jurisdiction claims, and inconsistent numbers across documents. Those are not cosmetic misses. Those are the mistakes that make a human reviewer spend the next three hours wondering what else is wrong.

Opus 4.8 was meaningfully better at not creating that mess.

The weakness was the visual layer. The central Market Creation Funnel visual was not good enough. It had fragile labels, awkward connectors, weak hierarchy, and the kind of pasted-in AI artifact that makes a deck feel less trustworthy even when the underlying thinking is fine.




That tells me exactly how I would use Opus 4.8 on a consulting-style packet.

I would trust it more than Opus 4.7 for source discipline, reconciliation, and legal ambiguity. I would still inspect the artifact before sending anything to a client or executive. If the work includes a board deck, dashboard, landing page, or diagram, I would assume the visual pass needs either a specialist model, a human designer, or a separate QA run.

The model won the task, but the review job remained.

Test 2: Car Wash operations
Score: Opus 4.8 at 86, GPT-5.5 at 55, Opus 4.7 at 48.




For executives and technical leaders, this is the most important result in the suite.

The Car Wash test is a dirty operational data migration. It has ghost records, orphaned orders, typoed customer information, enum variants, image-derived receipts, source files, provenance problems, conflicts, and records that should not be promoted into canonical data.

Most companies have this kind of work. It does not look impressive in a demo. It is not the thing a lab puts on stage. But it is everywhere: finance cleanup, CRM cleanup, invoice reconciliation, support-ticket migration, customer deduping, contract ingestion, compliance review, ERP cleanup.

This test answers the question, “Does the model know what not to do?”

Opus 4.8 handled the core traps. Ghost and test records were rejected. The orphaned Terrence Blackwood order stayed orphaned instead of becoming a fake canonical customer. A severe conflict on SVC-007 was surfaced instead of smoothed over. Typo names were merged correctly. Every job and payment carried source IDs. The package preserved 467 source files and 5,657 source records.

It’s not glamorous — it is the work.




The output also included a real reviewer workflow. The static UI showed conflicts, rejected records, source inventory, high-priority receivables flags, and review queues. The documentation was candid about review-grade revenue, reconciliation gaps, source recovery limits, and sensitive-file handling.

That candor is one of the strongest signals in the run.

A weaker model tries to make the result look finished. A better operational model knows the difference between finished, reviewable, and blocked. It knows that a revenue number with unresolved source gaps is not the same thing as a final revenue number. It knows that a suspicious record should go to a queue, not a spreadsheet cell that looks official because the model needed somewhere to put it.

Opus 4.8 still missed things. Department and role normalization were not implemented as first-class canonical data even though department values existed in recovered JSON source records. Some image-derived multi-service receipts put the full receipt amount on each service line, creating a risk of inflated billed totals. The mobile UI clipped navigation and metric cards. One source-file count created an audit-ledger inconsistency. OCR remained best-effort.

Those misses do not dismiss the result. They define the review plan.

If I were using Opus 4.8 for operational cleanup, I would not ask it to “clean the data” and accept a finished spreadsheet. I would ask it to build the cleanup system: preserve provenance, reject known bad records, surface conflicts, prove the canaries, and label unresolved items for human review.

On that job, Opus 4.8 looked unusually strong.

Test 3: Brick
Score: Opus 4.8 at 82.




The Brick test asks the model to create four LEGO-style builds from prompt to part list to runnable browser guide. It tests spatial reasoning, consistency across instructions and rendered output, physical plausibility, and whether the model can keep large builds from turning into decorative nonsense.

Opus 4.8 produced the strongest Brick result I have seen so far.

It completed all four prompts as separate runnable, data-driven animated assembly guides. It passed hard structural validators. It produced screenshots and kept the piece counts in range. It used a single source of truth so the kit spec drove the manifest, the instructions, the final model, and the animation.




The most useful part was the repair behavior.

The runner reported that repeated piece-count failures were detected, generator logic was revised, and final outputs were brought back into range. That is the kind of behavior I want from an agent: not just producing an artifact, but noticing when the artifact violates a hard constraint and revising the machinery that produced it.

The caveat is physical reality.

The output was internally structured and validated, but physical buildability was not fully proven. Some support and collision assumptions still need human brick-design review. The large airship depended on mooring and support assumptions. Some build steps added large batches of parts. Some raw model evidence was partial.

So I would not say, “Opus 4.8 can design production LEGO sets.”

I would say, “Opus 4.8 can generate a complex spatial artifact with a coherent internal structure, runnable instructions, and constraint-aware self-repair. If the artifact has to work in the physical world, it still needs expert review.”

That distinction is going to matter well beyond toy bricks.

AI systems are getting good at producing plausible operational artifacts. The human job is increasingly to know which parts of “plausible” have actually been tested.

Test 4: Artemis II visualization
Score: Opus 4.8 at 76, GPT-5.5 at 79, Opus 4.7 at 60.




Artemis is the test that keeps the article honest.

The task asks for a fact sheet plus an interactive 3D visualization of the Artemis II mission. The model has to handle source integrity, mission facts, timeline, visual staging, playback, camera controls, and the hard-to-dramatize parts of the mission: launch, staging, trans-lunar injection, lunar flyby, re-entry, splashdown, and recovery.

Opus 4.8 produced a complete package. It had a fact sheet, source list, offline visualization, documentation, screenshots, and validation evidence. The mission facts mostly aligned with NASA, CSA, and ESA sources. It used confidence tagging to separate official, secondary, and approximate data. The visualization had 14 phases, playback, a scrubber, event stepping, orbit and follow camera modes, a HUD, and local Three.js assets.




That is a good run, but not enough to win.

GPT-5.5 still beat it.

The reason was not factual safety. Opus 4.8 was safer than Opus 4.7. The issue was presentation. The visualization was too schematic. Splashdown and recovery did not read as distinct scenes. Later mission beats felt repetitive. Some central flyby and max-distance claims could have used stronger NASA primary support. Mobile framing pushed content partly off-screen.




The comparison to Opus 4.7 is useful. Opus 4.7 was more cinematic. It had a stronger visual feel. But it had source problems: missing traceable URLs, a CubeSat claim that contradicted NASA primary sources, timing issues, and unsupported colorful details.

So Opus 4.8 moved in the direction I want for trust. It moved backward in a place where Claude has often felt strong: visual taste and front-end presentation.

That does not make Opus 4.8 worse. It tells you how to route the work.

For a sourced visualization, I would use Opus 4.8 for the source packet and factual structure. I would not trust the visual result without inspection. If the visual experience matters, I would run a separate design pass and then a final source-preserving QA pass.

For serious AI work, this is the new routing habit: split the job by failure mode.

What the benchmark actually says
The suite says Opus 4.8 is excellent.

It also says “excellent” is not the same thing as “automatic default.”

The real improvement over Opus 4.7 is that Opus 4.8 behaves better around messy work. It preserves sources. It catches more traps. It is more careful about reviewability. It can self-repair against constraints. It is less willing to launder uncertainty into a finished-looking artifact.

Those are the exact things that make a model useful for paid work, internal operations, and executive analysis.

The regressions are not imaginary. Visual output was not reliably ahead. The Artemis task went to GPT-5.5. And the outside Vending-Bench results show that effort settings can change long-horizon behavior in ways that are not intuitive.

I would not turn that average score into a procurement strategy, or even a personal workflow strategy.

I would use the leaderboard as a starting point.

Then I would test the work.

High, extra, and max: how I would use Opus 4.8
The easiest mistake with Opus 4.8 is assuming max effort means best effort.

Anthropic says Opus 4.8 defaults to high effort. Users can choose extra or max. Anthropic recommends extra for difficult tasks and long-running async workflows.

At first glance, it looks like a normal slider: harder task, more effort.

But long-running agent work is not always helped by more internal thinking. If the model spends too many tokens reasoning, it can hit context limits sooner, compact more often, and lose practical continuity. On a short proof or a narrow review, that tradeoff may be worth it. On a long business simulation, it may not be.

Andon Labs found exactly that kind of problem on Vending-Bench. Opus 4.8 was a step forward on some alignment dimensions, but a step back on several business-performance metrics. In their Vending-Bench Arena, Opus 4.8 lost to GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.7. More importantly, Opus 4.8 performed better at high effort than at max effort.

Their hypothesis is simple enough to be useful: max effort burned far more reasoning tokens, triggered more compactions, and caused the agent to forget more of the business state. They found Opus 4.8 on max used about five times more reasoning tokens than Opus 4.8 on high and Opus 4.7 on max, leading to more than twice as many compactions.

That does not prove max is bad. It means you should not treat max as best. It is a specific operating mode with a specific failure risk.

This is how I would use the modes.

Use high as the default
High is where I would start for most real work:

Long-form writing from source material.

Research synthesis.

Consulting-style packets.

Messy operational data cleanup.

First drafts of serious internal artifacts.

Source-grounded reports.

Coding assistance where the task has multiple steps.

Any job where the model needs to remember what it already did.

High gives you strong reasoning without immediately turning the task into a context-management problem. It is also Anthropic’s default, which matters because defaults usually reflect the company’s own view of the best quality-to-friction tradeoff.

If you do not know which effort setting to use, use high.

Use extra for hard, bounded work
Extra is where I would go when the task is difficult and the answer is worth the additional token spend.

Examples:

A hard code change with acceptance tests.

A migration plan where the constraints are known.

A source-heavy review before a human signs off.

A complex architecture decision.

A Claude Code workflow that can be split into pieces and verified.

Extra makes sense when the model benefits from more reasoning and the work has enough structure to keep that reasoning anchored.

Use max sparingly
Max is for narrow, high-value thinking where context churn is unlikely to hurt you.

Examples:

Adversarial review of a plan.

A second-opinion pass on a technical argument.

A bounded proof or reasoning problem.

A final risk review where the source set is controlled.

I would not use max as my default for long-running agentic work until I had tested it on my own tasks. I would especially avoid it for work where the model has to carry a lot of evolving state over time.

If you turn on max and the model gets slower, more verbose, more self-conscious, and less practically useful, do not argue with the label. Turn it back down.

Where Opus 4.8 regresses or gets weird
I see four risk areas.

The first is visual and front-end output.

Opus 4.8 did strong underlying work in Dingo and Artemis, but both runs had presentation problems. The Dingo funnel visual was weak. Artemis was safer but less visually effective than the Opus 4.7 run. GPT-5.5 beat Opus 4.8 on the Artemis task.

This surprised me because Claude has often been strong for writing, product taste, and front-end feel. I still think those strengths are real in many everyday cases. But the benchmark result is a reminder not to rely on lineage reputation. Look at the artifact.

The second is effort sensitivity.

Vending-Bench is the clearest warning. High beat max on Opus 4.8 in that long-horizon business task. The likely reason was not philosophical. It was mechanical: reasoning tokens, compaction, and state loss.

That means effort setting is now part of model selection. It is not an afterthought.

The third is the alignment-versus-operations tradeoff.

Andon Labs found Opus 4.8 was better behaved in some ways but worse at running the vending business. The nuance matters. They still saw price-fixing and market-allocation collusion, though less frequently than with prior models, and they did not find the same deceptive or power-seeking behavior they had seen in earlier Claude models and Mythos Preview. At the same time, Opus 4.8 made worse business decisions on the benchmark.

I do not want models that win by colluding, lying, or exploiting their environment. A lower score caused by better behavior may be a good thing. But poor inventory management, scams, overpricing, and losing track of business state are not moral virtues. They are operational failures.

So your evals need to separate honest behavior from effective behavior. You want both.

The fourth is harness fit.

By harness I mean the product around the model: the file access, the tool calls, the permissions, the memory, the compaction behavior, the rate limits, and the workflow that turns a model response into an accepted artifact.

Opus 4.8 in Claude Code is not the same experience as Opus 4.8 through an API. Opus 4.8 in a chat UI is not the same as Opus 4.8 in a workflow that can inspect files, run tools, preserve state, and verify outputs. GPT-5.5 as a raw model is not the same thing as GPT-5.5 inside Codex with local files, browser tools, persistent goals, and an execution loop.

A chat window, a coding agent, and a local operator can expose the same model to different information and different failure modes. The model name may be identical. The work experience is not.

Why I still use Codex/5.5 for a lot of daily work
The benchmark table makes this next part sound contradictory.

Opus 4.8 won the suite. I am still using Codex/5.5 for a lot of my daily work.

Not because I think Opus 4.8 is weak. It is not weak. The suite says the opposite.

Because my daily work is not a detached prompt. It is a long-running operating surface.

I ask agents to find source material across my machine. I ask them to read attachments, inspect local files, use browser tools, work across projects, verify generated documents, update CMP assets, maintain goals, run shell commands, and keep going when the job takes hours instead of minutes.

For that kind of work, the harness decides a lot.

Codex/5.5 fits my current workflow because it can operate across the real work surface. It can read the files that matter. It can run commands. It can verify the actual artifact instead of trusting a filename and use browser and local tools when the job requires it. It can keep a goal alive and work through a multi-step deliverable.

I keep reaching for it because fewer handoffs get dropped between the request and the finished work.

I do not mean that OpenAI has permanently beaten Anthropic. I do not even mean that GPT-5.5 is generally smarter than Opus 4.8. The benchmark average says otherwise.

It is a claim about fit.

Claude Code’s dynamic workflows are important for the same reason. Anthropic is clearly building around long-running agent work: plan the workflow, split it across subagents, verify outputs, and return a coordinated result. The Bun port example is exactly the kind of frontier workload that deserves attention: a large migration, many lines of code, a real test suite, and a long time horizon.

That is the right direction for Claude.

I am not trying to turn this into “Claude wins” or “Codex wins.” The competition has moved into the workflow around the model. The model still matters. But the file system, tools, state, evals, permissions, and verification loop now matter enough to change the recommendation.

For my day-to-day work in June 2026, Codex/5.5 is often the better fit.

For careful writing, source-grounded synthesis, messy operational review, and some Claude Code workflows, Opus 4.8 may be the better model.

The answer changes by job.

My model-selection guide
If you are trying to choose between Opus 4.8, Codex/5.5, GPT-5.5, and older Claude models, I would route work this way.

Use Opus 4.8 when the work needs careful judgment
Use Opus 4.8 for:

Source-grounded writing.

Long-form synthesis.

Professional knowledge-work packets.

Messy operational data review.

Tasks with legal, ethical, or provenance traps.

Work where uncertainty should be surfaced instead of hidden.

Claude Code workflows where the job can be decomposed and verified.

I would start on high and move to extra if the task is hard and bounded. I would use max only with a reason.

Use Codex/5.5 when the work needs the local operating surface
Use Codex/5.5 when the task depends on:

Actual files on your machine.

Shell execution.

Browser or computer tools.

Repo changes and tests.

Local verification.

Multiple long-running workstreams.

Automations.

CMP or workflow updates.

Goal persistence.

The case for Codex/5.5 here is straightforward: it is fewer dropped handoffs between the model and the work.

Use GPT-5.5 as a strong reasoning or review pass
Use GPT-5.5 when you want:

A different reasoning style.

A second model to catch assumptions.

Strong structured review.

Visual or interactive work where your own tests show it performs well.

A cross-check against Claude’s source packet or prose choices.

The Artemis result is the reminder here. Opus 4.8 won the average. GPT-5.5 still won a specific task. That is why routing beats brand loyalty.

Use Opus 4.7 only for a known regression case
I would not make Opus 4.7 the default. Opus 4.8 is a major improvement in our suite.

But if your own eval shows Opus 4.7 beating 4.8 on a specific long-horizon workload, believe the eval. The Vending-Bench result is enough to make that a real possibility.

Newer does not always mean better for every job.

A model-selection prompt you can use
If you want a model to help you route a task, use this.

You are helping me choose the right AI model and workflow for a specific job.

Do not recommend a model because it is generally strongest. Recommend based on the job.

Ask me only the minimum questions needed to understand:
- What I need done.
- What source material the job depends on.
- Whether the work is short, long-running, or multi-stage.
- Whether the output needs writing quality, technical correctness, visual quality, operational judgment, or all of these.
- Whether the work needs local files, browser/computer use, shell execution, repo changes, or external tools.
- Whether a human will review the result before it is used.
- Whether cost, latency, rate limits, or state loss matter.

Then produce:
- Recommended model and workflow.
- Recommended reasoning effort.
- Why this choice fits the job.
- What a second-pass model should check.
- What canaries or acceptance tests should be run.
- What would make you change the recommendation.

Use these defaults:
- Use Claude Opus 4.8 high for source-grounded writing, careful synthesis, and messy knowledge work.
- Use Opus 4.8 extra for difficult bounded work where the output can be verified.
- Use Opus 4.8 max only for narrow, high-value reasoning or review where context churn is unlikely to hurt the result.
- Use Codex/5.5 when the job depends on local files, shell execution, browser/computer tools, long-running workflows, repo work, automations, or multiple parallel tasks.
- Use a second model to review high-stakes work.

Begin by asking your questions.
What builders should do
Builders should stop treating model selection as a one-time preference.

Keep a small eval set of real work. Not toy prompts. Real work.

Pick three to five tasks that represent your world:

One writing or synthesis task.

One messy data or source-reconciliation task.

One coding or repo task.

One visual or artifact-generation task.

One long-running task where state can get lost.

Run them against the models and harnesses you are considering. Score the outputs on the things that actually matter:

Correctness.

Source discipline.

Review burden.

Time to accepted artifact.

Cost.

Failure behavior.

Visual quality when relevant.

Whether the model knew what it did not know.

Then route work based on that.

If Opus 4.8 wins your eval, use Opus 4.8. If Codex/5.5 wins your eval, use Codex. If the answer changes by task, build routing instead of pretending one model settled the question.

Also test effort settings. Do not assume high, extra, and max are just better, better, best. They are operating modes with tradeoffs. On some jobs, more reasoning helps. On some jobs, more reasoning burns the context the task needed.

And if you are building agentic workflows, make verification part of the design. A model that produces more work faster can still make your system worse if the review path cannot absorb the output.

Accepted output is the metric. Not model activity.

What technical leaders should do
Technical leaders should tie AI budget to outcomes, not model makers.

A lot of companies are still trying to pick a permanent winner. They want one contract to answer the strategy question. I understand the impulse. Procurement wants simplicity. Security wants fewer vendors. Finance wants a clean forecast.

But the model race is still moving, and the useful surface is expanding beyond the model itself.

If your AI plan depends on one lab staying permanently ahead, your plan is brittle.

Define the outcomes first:

Engineering migration throughput.

Time from ticket to tested PR.

Support resolution quality.

Finance reconciliation accuracy.

Sales research cycle time.

Legal review coverage.

Content production quality.

Human review burden.

Then ask which model and workflow produces accepted output at the best total cost.

Total cost is not just token price. It includes failed runs, retries, human review, integration work, rate-limit friction, vendor lock-in, data governance, workflow disruption, and the downstream work created by agents.

That last part is easy to miss.

Agents can create work faster than organizations can review it. If your team suddenly has ten times as many PRs, reports, support drafts, dashboard prototypes, or research packets, you have not automatically improved throughput. You may have moved the bottleneck to review.

The leadership job is not to buy intelligence. It is to build a system that turns intelligence into accepted work.

That means flexible contracts, internal evals, source truth, cost ledgers, review gates, and a clear decision about where humans sit in the loop.

The best teams will not be the ones that guessed the right model in June 2026. They will be the ones that can switch models without rebuilding the operating system.

What executives should not overcommit budget to
Executives should not overcommit budget to the idea that one model maker has permanently won.

Do not turn a benchmark table into a procurement plan.

Do not fund a giant contract without mapping it to specific accepted outputs.

Do not let a vendor demo become your operating architecture.

Do not measure success by seats provisioned, tokens consumed, or agent tasks launched.

Do not assume the highest reasoning setting produces the best work.

Do not assume the smartest model is the safest model for your workflow.

Do not assume the safest model is the most effective operator.

Do not assume an impressive benchmark means the tool fits your company.

The practical executive move is to keep the architecture flexible and tie spend to outcomes.

Your durable advantage is not access to one model. Everyone with a credit card can get access to strong models. The durable advantage is the system around them: your source data, evals, workflows, review gates, prompts, internal tools, integration layer, governance, cost tracking, and people who know how to use these systems without confusing output volume for progress.

The model makers will keep trading the lead.

Your company should not have to reorganize every time they do.

My bottom line
Opus 4.8 is a strong release.

It is the best model in our current strict benchmark suite. It is a major improvement over Opus 4.7 on messy work: source discipline, operational judgment, canary handling, provenance, self-repair, and careful synthesis.

I would use it seriously.

I would not use it blindly.

It can regress visually. It can behave differently across effort levels. Max can be worse than high on some long-running work. GPT-5.5 can still beat it on a specific task. Codex/5.5 can still fit my day-to-day operating workflow better because of the way the tool surrounds the model.

I am not saying this to diminish Opus 4.8. I am saying it because this is the practical state of AI work in 2026.

If you are a builder, run your own evals.

If you are a technical leader, buy outcomes.

If you are an executive, do not turn a model launch into a permanent budget commitment before you know where the work actually lands.

I would not phrase the decision as “Opus wins” or “Codex wins.”

You have to decide where the job should run.

Opus 4.8 makes that hard to ignore.

Use it where it is strong. Test it where it is uncertain. Keep your workflow flexible enough to change your mind.

Coming Up
Token burn is becoming one of the most important metrics in AI work, and most people aren't tracking theirs. On Friday, I'll break down why it matters, what it actually tells you about your workflow, and walk you through building your own dashboard so you can start measuring it.

This is a sharp piece, and you're right that we already cover the underlying idea — but we never *name* it, and a named problem is one people actually act on. Let me first separate what's genuinely new from what we already have, then make the changes.

Let me confirm a few exact anchors before editing.

Anchors confirmed. Here's my read, then the edits.

**What we already cover** (so I won't duplicate): source discipline/provenance (evidence levels §4.4, source levels §8.7.4), not laundering uncertainty (§10), review friction (§4.7), review-by-exception (§11), budget/total-cost (§4.8, §8.10.1), self-repair (§3.7). Nate's piece validates a lot of our design.

**What's genuinely new and worth taking:**
1. **A name for the problem** — "the work pile problem," and the reframe *accepted output is the metric, not produced output.* We imply this (§17 rule 10) but never say it crisply.
2. **"Finished vs reviewable vs blocked"** — honest deliverable-state labeling (distinct from our claim-level evidence levels).
3. **Review burden as a measured metric** — directly instruments the work pile problem.
4. *(propose, not auto-add)* **Model + reasoning-effort routing** (max ≠ best for long-horizon agents) and **a real eval set** for the agents.

Making the Tier-1 changes now:

Now add a glossary entry for the new named concept, then bump the version.

Done — the document is now **v2.1** and uses the "work pile problem" language throughout.

**What I added (Tier 1):**
- **New principle §4.9 — "Accepted output is the goal, not produced output (the work pile problem)."** Names the problem in Nate's exact terms, states that the human's attention is the scarcest resource, and gives three implications: throttle production to review capacity, label work honestly, and count accepted output + review burden.
- **§11 KPIs** — added two human-headline metrics: **Human Review Burden** and **Accepted Output Rate**, and rewrote the closing line to "count accepted output, not activity… a rising backlog is the work pile problem, not progress."
- **§10.2** — new agent restriction: must label every deliverable **final / reviewable / blocked**, and may not present reviewable or blocked work as final (Nate's "knows the difference between finished, reviewable, and blocked").
- **§17 rulebook** — new rule 11: *progress is measured in accepted output; a growing backlog is the work pile problem, not productivity.*
- **Glossary** — entries for **Work pile problem** and **Accepted output**.

**Two I deliberately did *not* auto-add — your call:**

1. **Model + reasoning-effort routing.** Nate's strongest operational insight: pick the model *and* the effort level per task, and higher reasoning isn't always better — on long-horizon agent work, more reasoning can burn context and lose state (the Vending-Bench finding). I'd write this **model-agnostic** (no version names, so it doesn't date) as a short §8.11, since you're already running agents and this directly affects cost and reliability.
2. **A real eval set for the agents.** Keep ~5 real tasks, score them on correctness, source discipline, **review burden**, time-to-accepted, cost, and failure behavior — and *separate honest behavior from effective behavior*. This is genuinely worth it because it also closes the open gap we noted: it gives the "policy compliance score" an actual measurement method.

Both are real improvements and fit the document. Want me to add §8.11 (routing) and the eval-set practice (as §8.10.5)? I'd recommend yes to both — they're the parts of Nate's piece that make an agent *company*, not just a model choice, more robust.

Awesome! I just had a look at the agent prompts, and I believe for the CEO agent, we have to include that it should communicate to the board in a clear way that is readable for humans. 

We have a little bit of that already, but it's not enough in my experience.

What I had to add to the prompt the last time I ran an agency, in order to make the output of the CEO even understandable for me, and to avoid the agent sending me around different tickets that are referenced, which I really cannot keep in my head as a human being,, is the following: "Tone
Direct, calm, and economical.
No filler, no executive theater, no vague enthusiasm.
Name the decision, the tradeoff, and the next move.
Write in plain English for the operator, not in boardroom language.
Make answers self-contained so the reader does not need to hunt through other tickets to understand what changed, what is true, and what to do next.
When a factual claim depends on the current repo or workspace state, verify it first. Do not repeat subordinate claims as facts until you have checked them yourself or clearly labeled them as unverified.
If a prior claim was wrong, correct it directly and explicitly instead of hiding behind process language.
When you tell the operator how to do something, distinguish clearly between actions they can take from the chat/UI and actions that require a VPS-side or board-authorized actor. Do not talk as if the operator is logged into the server unless you have verified that."

Also, I believe at some point in my previous experiments, I agreed with the agents that it would make sense to add a company philosophy to the agents.md of every agent, so they all have one guardrail getting them in the same direction. 

However, I don't know whether or not that added value. I just noticed there is nothing like that in our prompts, and I wonder: should we have something or not?
answer:
Two good catches. Let me handle them — first by looking at the current base and CEO prompts so I edit precisely.

I can see exactly what's going on. Two useful findings:

1. **Your pasted "Tone" block is already in the base prompt** (§8.6.1, lines 843–851) — it applies to every agent. So the gap isn't that it's missing; it's that the **CEO prompt itself is thin** ("do not produce boardroom prose" is the only line), and the CEO is precisely the agent whose entire job is talking to you. Your real pain — being sent to chase referenced tickets — needs to be hammered home *specifically for the CEO*, with a concrete rule, not left to the general base tone.

2. On philosophy: you're right that there's nothing like it. My recommendation below.

Let me strengthen the CEO prompt first:

Now the **company philosophy** question — my honest take:

**Yes, it's worth having — but do it once, in the base prompt that all agents inherit, not copied into each agent's file.** Putting it per-agent (what you did before) means N copies to keep in sync and more prompt bloat; the base prompt is the single inheritance point, so one block there gives every agent the same compass. The reason it may have felt like it "didn't add value" before is the usual failure mode: philosophy that's vague ("be excellent," "delight the customer") is noise an LLM ignores. It earns its place only if it's **concrete and decision-shaping** — tenets an agent can actually apply when the SOP doesn't cover a situation.

So I'd add a tight 6-line block that *distills* what's already in §4 (principles) and §17 (rulebook) into a working compass. I've added it to the base prompt:

The document is now **v2.3**. Summary of the two changes:

**CEO communication (§8.6.2) — strengthened.** Added a dedicated "Communication to the operator (the board)" block that makes clear human-readable reporting the CEO's *core deliverable*, with your hard-won rules baked in — the key one being: **every report stands alone; if it references a ticket, summarize that ticket inline; never send the operator chasing another ticket/file/thread.** Plus verify-before-asserting, correct-errors-explicitly, and the chat-UI-vs-server distinction, ending with "if the operator would have to ask 'what does this refer to?', the report is not done."

**Company philosophy (§8.6.1) — added, once, in the base prompt.** A 6-line concrete compass (trust is the product; evidence over confidence; accepted output not produced; protect the operator's attention; procedure over improvisation; SAP-specific credibility) — a distillation of §4 and §17. Because it's in the *base* prompt, every agent inherits it; no per-agent duplication to maintain.

**My recommendation on the philosophy, stated plainly:** keep it. The version that "didn't add value" before was almost certainly vague-values phrasing; this one is decision-shaping (it tells an agent how to choose when the SOP is silent). It costs six lines per run and gives you the single shared direction you wanted. If it doesn't earn its keep once you see agents run, it's trivial to cut — but I'd bet it reduces drift.

Let me record your communication preference so I apply it to how I report to you too, not just the agents.

Both changes are in (v2.3), and I've noted your "self-contained, plain-English, no cross-reference chasing" preference so I hold *my own* reports to you to the same standard going forward — not just the CEO agent.

Quick recap of where the document stands, self-contained so you don't have to scroll back:
- **CEO prompt (§8.6.2):** now treats clear human reporting as its core job, with the inline-ticket-summary rule front and center.
- **Base prompt (§8.6.1):** now carries a 6-line shared philosophy that every agent inherits — my recommendation is to keep it, since it's concrete enough to shape decisions.

Still pending your call from earlier (not lost): **§8.11 model/effort routing** and the **eval-set practice (§8.10.5)**. Otherwise the document is in good shape for you to set a company up against it.

## Which is better: separate sessions or do it here?

**Separate, focused session per kit — one for OpenClaw, one for Hermes.** Reasons that actually matter:

- **Each kit is its own repo with its own `CLAUDE.md`, GSD enforcement, conventions, and memory.** In *this* session the loaded project instructions are Paperclip's. ````markdown
# Task: collapse the 3-command start into a single `curl … | bash` one-liner

## Goal
Match the **Paperclip DevOps Kit**'s one-line install. Today this kit needs three
steps (run the installer, `cd … && claude`, then paste `Read 00-master-prompt.md
and start.`). Make `curl -fsSL "<install gist raw URL>" | bash` do all three: install
the kit, then drop the operator straight into Claude already running onboarding.

## Reference implementation (read it first)
The Paperclip kit is a sibling repo at `c:\Dev\paperclip-devops-kit`. Read
`assets/install.sh` **Section 5 ("Launch the onboarding")** — the load-bearing block is:

```bash
CLAUDE_BIN="$HOME/.local/bin/claude"
command -v "$CLAUDE_BIN" >/dev/null 2>&1 || CLAUDE_BIN="$(command -v claude || echo claude)"

if [ -r /dev/tty ]; then
  cd "$KIT_DIR"
  exec "$CLAUDE_BIN" "Read 00-master-prompt.md and start." < /dev/tty
fi
# …otherwise fall through to the printed "Next: cd … && claude" summary.
```

**Why `< /dev/tty` is non-negotiable:** when the script runs via `curl | bash`, stdin is
the pipe, not the keyboard. Re-attaching `/dev/tty` hands the interactive Claude session a
real terminal. Without it the launched Claude gets EOF on stdin and dies immediately. This
trick is the whole reason Paperclip is one-liner-able.

## What to change in THIS kit
1. **`assets/install.sh`** — replace the summary-only ending so that, when `/dev/tty` is
